comments.text:
If your village shut its own reef for a year, would you wait, or would the family income win? What would you want to know first? ▶ Watch next:
👉Chuuk | How Life Works in a Lagoon Full of Sunken Warships: https://youtu.be/aigIXaJ674A
👉Lanai | How Life Works Where One Billionaire Owns 98% of the Land: https://youtu.be/7NJulb7aRTk
👉Banda | How Life Works Where an Active Volcano Is the Next-Door Neighbor: https://youtu.be/XhYMhvt9Afw
👉Mackinac | How Life Works When Ice Stops Michigan's Ferries: https://youtu.be/j27LNtH9GvA
👉Lived in Raja Ampat or visited? Tell us what we got right or missed.

Two sides of one closed reef: families give up months, often a year, of the catch that sells (sea cucumber, trochus, lobster) so the reef can refill, and the whole village reopens it together on one morning. Is closing your own sea a smart bet or a hard price for a family that needs money now? And on the nickel question at Gag Island, where four of five permits were revoked on 10 June 2025 and one stayed, which weighs more for you: state revenue and jobs, or protection for the reef? What is the hardest part for you?

comments.author: @travellives
comments.text: Funny how Western tourists pay $60 'conservation fees' to dive here while driving EVs powered by nickel mined right next door on Gag Island.

replies.author: @RemoteEarthJourneys
replies.text: You raise an important point about the environmental costs of travel. Conservation fees and tourism's wider footprint deserve thoughtful scrutiny, especially in places as fragile as Raja Ampat. Thanks for adding that perspective.

comments.author: @Kenna-g9z
comments.text: Recording 374 fish species on a single dive at Cape Kri and housing 75% of the world's hard corals... Raja Ampat isn't just a reef, it's Earth's marine ark.

replies.author: @RemoteEarthJourneys
replies.text: The marine life around Raja Ampat is extraordinary, and those reefs are worth protecting. 🐠 Have you had a chance to dive there yourself?

comments.author: @travelintolifeus
comments.text: I would love to understand what living in Raja Ampat is really like, where the sea provides food, transportation, and a way of life. The tradition of temporarily closing fishing areas shows remarkable patience and respect for the ocean. That's a lesson the rest of the world could learn from.

replies.author: @RemoteEarthJourneys
replies.text: Beautifully said. The practice of allowing fishing grounds time to recover shows how closely local life is tied to a healthy sea. 🌊 Which part of village life would you most like to see up close?

comments.author: @lifeonearth68
comments.text: When your boat is basically your car and gas costs that much, even a simple trip to the store becomes a big decision🤔🤔. Anyone living on these islands know how often families usually travel between villages? 🌏🏝

replies.author: @RemoteEarthJourneys
replies.text: Great question. Travel frequency can depend on the island, weather and the reason for the trip. If someone from the area is watching, we'd love to hear their firsthand experience.

comments.text: Oh my, those turquoise waters, the little islands around Piaynemo, and the incredible views from Wayag look almost unreal. Anyone wants to go snorkeling? <3

replies.author: @RemoteEarthJourneys
replies.text: Those waters are extraordinary! 🐠 Snorkeling there would be unforgettable. Would you rather explore the coral gardens or look for manta rays?

comments.author: @MrCuriousEN
comments.text: Sasi is fascinating because it turns conservation into a community economic decision rather than an outside rule. 🌊🐚 Closing a reef means giving up income today in the hope of having more tomorrow, which is much harder than it sounds when families depend directly on the sea. The fact that the system existed long before modern conservation programs makes it even more interesting.
